title: Successful rechallenge with almonertinib and corticosteroids after gefitinib-induced interstitial lung disease: A case report and literature review.
authors: Liu J, Wei T, Bao Z et al.
abstract:
RATIONALE: First-generation epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) are highly effective in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC); however, drug-induced interstitial lung disease (ILD) remains a rare but potentially fatal adverse event. The safety and efficacy of EGFR-TKI rechallenge - either with the same agent or an alternative one - following ILD resolution are not established and represent a significant clinical knowledge gap.
PATIENT CONCERNS: A 53-year-old never-smoking woman with stage IV lung adenocarcinoma - detected to harbor an L858R mutation in exon 21 of the EGFR gene - developed progressive dyspnea and hypoxemia after 2 months of first-line gefitinib therapy, despite confirmed initial radiographic and clinical response.
DIAGNOSES: The patient was diagnosed with grade 3 gefitinib-associated ILD.
INTERVENTIONS: With the discontinuation of gefitinib, the patient was given methylprednisolone to resolve ILD. To control advanced lung adenocarcinoma progression, the patient was subjected to 6 cycles of treatment using pemetrexed, carboplatin, and bevacizumab, with measurable tumor shrinkage, followed by maintenance therapy with bevacizumab. Furthermore, given the tumor progression 14 months later, the patient was prescribed docetaxel plus bevacizumab to restore control. Ten months later, the patient experienced disease progression and strongly requested to use EGFR-TKIs again given prior response to EGFR-TKI. The patient was rechallenged with almonertinib, a third-generation EGFR-TKI, and methylprednisolone.
OUTCOMES: The patient had measurable tumor shrinkage, with sustained tumor control and no recurrence of pulmonary toxicity. As of last follow-up, she maintained progression-free survival for approximately 8 months on almonertinib.
LESSONS: This case provides a hypothesis-generating observation, illustrating feasibility only in highly‑selected patients with EGFR‑mutant NSCLC and prior severe TKI‑related ILD. With prophylactic corticosteroids and rigorous surveillance, third‑generation EGFR‑TKI may represent a tentative clinical option for such patients, but general safety cannot be inferred from this single case.

title: Thoracic ultrasound for assessing chest wall invasion in lung cancer with suspected chest wall involvement: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
AIM: This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of thoracic ultrasound for detecting chest wall invasion in patients with lung cancer and suspected chest wall involvement, using surgical and/or histopathologic findings as the reference standard.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception through June 2026 for studies of thoracic ultrasound in patients with suspected chest wall invasion by lung cancer. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) were pooled separately using random-intercept logistic models. Heterogeneity was quantified with I2, and leave-one-out analyses assessed robustness. The review followed PRISMA-DTA and was prospectively registered in PROSPERO.
RESULTS: Four studies comprising 249 enrolled patients were included; 246 patients contributed to diagnostic accuracy analyses. Pooled sensitivity was 89.8% (95% CI, 62.4%-97.9%; I2 = 32.5%), and pooled specificity was 94.0% (95% CI, 84.1%-97.9%; I2 = 63.9%). Pooled PPV and NPV were 85.5% (95% CI, 74.4%-92.3%; I2 = 35.9%) and 96.3% (95% CI, 82.4%-99.3%; I2 = 17.0%), respectively. Leave-one-out analyses did not materially alter the findings.
CONCLUSION: Thoracic ultrasound showed favourable pooled diagnostic performance for detecting chest wall invasion in selected patients with lung cancer and may complement preoperative imaging, particularly by increasing confidence in the absence of invasion. The limited evidence base, variability in diagnostic criteria and operator experience, and heterogeneity in specificity warrant cautious interpretation and validation in larger prospective studies using standardised protocols.

title: Pulmonary sarcomatoid carcinoma with METex14 mutation and high PD-L1: A case report.
abstract:
RATIONALE: Pulmonary sarcomatoid carcinoma (PSC) is a rare and aggressive subtype of lung cancer, posing diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. Cases of PSC harboring both MET exon 14 skipping (METex14) mutation and high PD-L1 expression are rarely documented, and reports detailing multimodal treatment involving surgery, chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy in such patients are even scarcer.
PATIENT CONCERNS: A 54-year-old man presented with a persistent cough for over half a month. He was previously healthy. Physical examination revealed diminished breath sounds in the right upper lung.
DIAGNOSES: Initial bronchoscopic biopsy suggested inflammation, and computed tomography (CT)-guided lung biopsy showed atypical giant cells but was inconclusive. Following multidisciplinary team discussion, the patient underwent surgical resection. Postoperative pathology confirmed pleomorphic carcinoma (sarcomatoid carcinoma). Subsequent genetic testing identified a METex14 mutation with high PD-L1 expression (Tumor Proportion Score ≥ 50%). The final diagnosis was stage IIIB (T4N2M0) right PSC, MET-positive, PD-L1-positive.
INTERVENTIONS: The initial treatment plan included 1 cycle of toripalimab (an anti-PD-1 antibody) combined with docetaxel and lobaplatin chemotherapy. This was subsequently adjusted to boretinib (a MET inhibitor) targeted therapy combined with docetaxel and lobaplatin chemotherapy.
OUTCOMES: The patient achieved and maintained a partial response (PR) for over 6 months of follow-up. Symptoms including cough resolved, and his general condition remained good with satisfactory appetite and sleep.
LESSONS: This case underscores the diagnostic difficulty of PSC, which is prone to misdiagnosis and exhibits rapid growth. Surgery may not be appropriate for unresectable stage IIIB PSC. Gene sequencing and PD-L1 testing are crucial as they expand therapeutic options for PSC patients. The optimal first-line therapy (targeted vs immunotherapy) for PSC with concurrent MET mutation and high PD-L1 expression remains undefined, warranting further exploration of combination strategies.

title: From Bench to Bedside Faster: How CAR-NK is Transforming Cancer Research.
authors: Singh S, Rathod B, Puri S
abstract: In recent years, chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy has emerged as an effective treatment for haematological malignancies, including lymphoma and leukaemia. However, its clinical application is associated with several challenges, including severe toxicities such as cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity, high manufacturing costs, prolonged production times, and delays associated with patient-specific manufacturing. These limitations have prompted the development of safer, more accessible immunotherapeutic alternatives. Chimeric antigen receptor natural killer (CAR-NK) cell therapy has emerged as a promising next-generation approach that may offer comparable antitumour activity with a potentially more favourable safety profile than CAR-T therapy. CAR-NK cells generally have a lower risk of severe cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity, as well as a substantially lower risk of graft-versus-host disease. Moreover, CAR-NK cells can be generated from allogeneic donor sources, supporting the development of off-the-shelf products that may reduce manufacturing time and costs. By combining antigen-specific tumour recognition with the innate cytotoxic mechanisms of natural killer cells, CAR-NK therapy may enhance tumour cell killing. Recent preclinical and clinical studies in haematological malignancies and solid tumours have reported promising antitumour activity and encouraging safety outcomes. Overall, CAR-NK therapy represents a promising complementary approach to CAR-T therapy, with potential advantages in safety and off-the-shelf manufacturing. However, CAR-T therapy has a more established clinical evidence base, particularly in haematological malignancies, and can achieve substantial in vivo expansion and durable remissions. The relative benefits of these platforms depend on the disease context, treatment objectives, and clinical evidence available for each product. Further comparative studies are needed to define their respective roles in cancer immunotherapy.

title: RESPONSE-ADAPTIVE STEREOTACTIC BODY RADIOTHERAPY BOOST AFTER CONCURRENT CHEMORADIOTHERAPY IN UNRESECTABLE STAGE III NSCLC: A PROSPECTIVE SINGLE-CENTRE COHORT STUDY.
authors: Kiraz E, Eroğlu C, Gündoğ M et al.
journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to escalate the dose to the residual primary tumor with an adaptive stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) boost after concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CRT) in unresectable stage III non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), and to explore, within this cohort, whether a higher cumulative dose to the residual primary was associated with better locoregional control (LRC) and whether this translated into a difference in overall survival (OS).
MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this single-center, prospective, single-arm cohort, 51 patients received concurrent CRT (50 Gy/25 fractions with weekly carboplatin and paclitaxel) followed by an adaptive boost (30 Gy/5 fractions to the residual primary, 10 Gy/5 fractions to residual nodes), without consolidation durvalumab. Doses were summed by deformable registration and reported as EQD2. Response was assessed at 3 months with FDG-PET/CT (PERCIST), and toxicity with CTCAE v5.0. Outcomes estimated by Kaplan-Meier; predictors by Cox regression.
RESULTS: At a median follow-up of 26 months, 2-year OS and LRC were 61.5% and 62.8%. The median PFS and DMFS were 13 and 16 months, and distant metastasis was the dominant failure pattern (41.2%). Cumulative dose below 94.77 Gy (EQD2) to the residual primary independently predicted worse LRC (HR 5.86), and a 3-month locoregional SUVmax ≥4.55 predicted worse LRC (HR 5.04). OS was independently associated with residual nodal volume, 3-month metabolic progression, and subsequent locoregional progression. Grade 3-4 pneumonitis occurred in 7.8%, grade 3 esophagitis in one patient (2%), and hemoptysis in five (9.8%).
CONCLUSION: The SBRT boost achieved encouraging locoregional control, including in bulky and node-advanced disease, without immunotherapy, and higher cumulative dose to the residual primary was associated with better locoregional control. Hemoptysis was the main safety concern and occurred predominantly in patients with pre-existing hemoptysis, supporting careful selection and strict bronchial constraints. Local escalation alone did not overcome the competing risk of distant failure.

title: Development and validation of a machine learning model and nomogram for predicting lung metastasis in thymoma: A population-based study.
authors: Wang C, Zeng Y, Zhang L et al.
abstract: The lung is the most frequent site of metastasis in patients with advanced thymoma. As a result, predicting the probability of lung metastasis and survival time has become a key focus in clinical practice. However, accurate prediction models are currently lacking. We collected complete data from 2004 to 2015 in the Surveillance, Epidemiology and End Results (SEER) database. Cox regression analysis was used to evaluate factors associated with the prognosis of thymoma patients. These independent prognostic factors were incorporated into the nomogram prognostic model. We validated the survival model by incorporating prognostic factors using receiver operating characteristic curves, calibration plots, C-index, and decision curve analysis curves. Synthetic minority over-sampling technique statistical methods were used to evaluate the machine learning model most suitable for building a predictive model of lung metastasis. Receiver operating characteristic curves, probability density plots, and confusion matrices were used to evaluate the performance of the prediction model. A total of 1776 thymoma patients were included in this study. Among them, age, sex, World Health Organization classification, Masaoka_Koga_Stage, surgery, chemotherapy, and lung metastasis were independent factors affecting metastasis. The machine learning model built by the gradient boosting machine algorithm performed best through internal data validation. Then, we used the gradient boosting machine algorithm to construct a web predictor of lung metastasis, and completed the construction and verification of the nomogram model. We developed an accessible online prediction tool (https://lung-metastasis---thymoma-ckfrve2aqrqr8tsdwbrqik.streamlit.app/) to evaluate the risk of lung metastasis. In addition, a predictive nomogram model was developed to predict the prognosis of patients with lung metastasis.
